lessonTitle: Solving the Discrete System: Tridiagonal, Direct and Iterative Solvers

blocks.text: A cooling fin 0.20 m long gives a one-dimensional temperature equation that a 4-interval grid turns into just three equations, solved by hand in minutes. A real model of the same fin with 100 000 intervals gives 100 000 equations; a dense solver would need about 80 GB of memory for the matrix, while a tridiagonal solver needs a few megabytes. The structure of the equations, not their number, decides which solver is sensible.

blocks.markdown: **Idea.** Discretising a boundary value problem on a grid gives a linear system $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{b}$. For one-dimensional diffusion each equation involves only a node and its two neighbours, so $\mathbf{A}$ is **tridiagonal**: non-zero only on the main diagonal and the two diagonals adjacent to it. Finite-element and finite-difference matrices in two and three dimensions are likewise **sparse**: almost all entries are zero. A good solver uses that structure.

blocks.title: Direct and iterative solvers
blocks.text: A **direct solver** (Gauss elimination, LU, Cholesky) finds $\mathbf{u}$ after a fixed, finite number of operations, apart from round-off. An **iterative solver** (Jacobi, Gauss-Seidel, conjugate gradients) starts from a guess and improves it repeatedly until the residual $\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}$ is below a tolerance; it never forms a factorisation.

blocks.markdown: **Model problem: a fin.** A thin fin with perimeter losses satisfies $\theta''=m^2\theta$, where $\theta=T-T_\infty$ (K) and $m$ (1/m) combines the film coefficient, perimeter, conductivity and cross-section. With uniform spacing $h$ the three-point formula gives, at each interior node, $\theta_{i-1}-(2+m^2h^2)\theta_i+\theta_{i+1}=0$. The known end values $\theta_0$ and $\theta_n$ move to the right-hand side of the first and last equations.

blocks.title: Solve a four-interval fin model
blocks.prompt: A fin of length $L=0.20$ m has $m=10$ m$^{-1}$, root excess temperature $\theta_0=75$ K and tip excess temperature $\theta_L=25$ K. Use $n=4$ intervals and solve the tridiagonal system. The exact solution is $\theta(x)=[\theta_0\sinh m(L-x)+\theta_L\sinh mx]/\sinh mL$.

steps.text: Grid and coefficient: $h=0.05$ m so $m^2h^2=0.25$ and the diagonal is $-2.25$.
Thomas algorithm, forward sweep: normalise each row by its pivot after eliminating the sub-diagonal. The modified super-diagonal $c'_i$ and right-hand side $d'_i$ are:
Exact values at $x=0.05,0.10,0.15$ m, and the difference.

blocks.answer: $\theta=(47.85,\ 32.65,\ 25.62)$ K, which is within 0.25 K of the exact values at every node. The cost was $O(n)$ operations; a dense solver would need $O(n^3)$.

blocks.markdown: **Why iterations grow with refinement.** For the 1D model problem the Jacobi iteration matrix has spectral radius $\rho=\cos(\pi h/L)\approx1-\pi^2h^2/(2L^2)$. The number of sweeps needed to cut the error by a factor $10^{-6}$ is about $\ln(10^{-6})/\ln\rho$, which grows like $1/h^2$: for 10, 100 and 1000 intervals about 275, 27991 and 2799603 sweeps. A direct tridiagonal solve costs the same few operations per unknown at any $n$. Gauss-Seidel halves the sweep count; conjugate gradients reduces the growth to $O(1/h)$, and multigrid removes it.

blocks.title: Convergence of Gauss-Seidel on the fin system
blocks.prompt: Apply Gauss-Seidel to the four-interval fin system written with positive diagonal: $2.25\theta_1-\theta_2=75$, $-\theta_1+2.25\theta_2-\theta_3=0$, $-\theta_2+2.25\theta_3=25$. Start from zero and report the iterates and the number of sweeps for the residual below $10^{-3}$ K.

steps.text: Update each unknown in turn using the newest values: $\theta_i\leftarrow(b_i-\sum_{j\ne i}A_{ij}\theta_j)/A_{ii}$. Sweep 1 gives
Continue until the largest residual $\max|b_i-\sum_jA_{ij}\theta_j|$ is below $10^{-3}$ K.

blocks.answer: Gauss-Seidel reaches the direct solution $(47.85,\ 32.65,\ 25.62)$ K after 12 sweeps. The system is strictly diagonally dominant ($2.25>1+1$), which guarantees convergence.

blocks.markdown: **Checking against the exact solution.** Compute the error $e(h)=|\theta_h-\theta_{exact}|$ at a fixed location (here mid-length $x=0.10$ m) for a sequence of grids and plot $\log e$ against $\log h$. A straight line of slope 2 confirms second-order accuracy. For this fin the errors at $n=4,8,16,32$ intervals are 0.25035, 0.06383, 0.01604, 0.00401 K, and each halving of $h$ divides the error by 3.92, 3.98, 3.99 (close to 4).

items: Assemble $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{b}$, put boundary values on the right-hand side, then choose the solver by structure and size.
Banded and tridiagonal systems should never be stored or factorised as dense matrices.
Iterative methods need a diagonally dominant or positive-definite matrix, a good starting guess and a stopping tolerance on the residual.
Verify with a case that has an exact solution and look at the log-log error plot: its slope is the order of accuracy.

blocks.title: Residual is not error
blocks.text: A small residual does not guarantee a small error when the matrix is ill-conditioned. With $\kappa(\mathbf{A})$ the condition number, the relative error is bounded by $\|\mathbf{e}\|/\|\mathbf{u}\|\le\kappa(\mathbf{A})\,\|\mathbf{r}\|/\|\mathbf{b}\|$, that is, by $\kappa$ times the relative residual, and it is at least $\tfrac{1}{\kappa}\|\mathbf{r}\|/\|\mathbf{b}\|$. Stopping an iteration on residual alone should be accompanied by a check on the solution.

points: One-dimensional diffusion with three-point differences gives a tridiagonal system, solved in $O(n)$ operations by the Thomas algorithm, while a dense solve costs $O(n^3)$ and $O(n^2)$ memory.
Iterative solvers cost less per step and keep the matrix sparse, but the number of sweeps grows as the grid is refined (about $1/h^2$ for Jacobi) unless a good method or preconditioner is used.
A discrete solution is checked against the exact solution; the slope of $\log e$ versus $\log h$ gives the order of accuracy, here close to 2.

questions.stem: Which condition on a matrix guarantees that the Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel iterations converge?

distractorRationale.b: A symmetric matrix can still give divergent Jacobi iterations; Gauss-Seidel additionally needs positive definiteness.
distractorRationale.c: Positive entries are neither necessary nor sufficient; the stencil has negative off-diagonals.
distractorRationale.d: A zero determinant means the matrix is singular and has no unique solution.

questions.explanation: Strict diagonal dominance guarantees $\rho<1$ for the iteration matrices of both methods. For the fin system the diagonal 2.25 exceeds the sum of the off-diagonals, 2, so the iteration converges.

questions.stem: A 1D diffusion problem is refined from 100 to 400 intervals and solved with Jacobi iteration to the same tolerance. Roughly how does the number of sweeps change?

options.text: It increases by about a factor of 16
It increases by about a factor of 4
It decreases by a factor of 4

questions.correctOptionText: It increases by about a factor of 16

distractorRationale.b: The count does not stay constant: the spectral radius approaches 1 as $h\to0$.
distractorRationale.c: A factor of 4 corresponds to a doubling of the intervals, not a quadrupling.
distractorRationale.d: The iteration slows down on finer grids; it does not speed up.

questions.explanation: The Jacobi spectral radius is $\cos(\pi h/L)\approx1-\pi^2h^2/(2L^2)$, so the number of sweeps $\propto1/h^2$. Quadrupling the number of intervals gives $4^2=16$ times more sweeps.

questions.stem: The error at a fixed point from a finite-difference solution is $4.0\times10^{-3}$ for $h=0.10$ and $1.0\times10^{-3}$ for $h=0.05$. What does the log-log plot of error against $h$ show?

options.text: A straight line of slope 2, indicating second-order convergence
A straight line of slope 1, indicating first-order convergence
A horizontal line, indicating no convergence
A line of slope 4, indicating fourth-order convergence

questions.correctOptionText: A straight line of slope 2, indicating second-order convergence

distractorRationale.b: A first-order method would show an error ratio of 2.
distractorRationale.c: A horizontal line would mean the error did not change.
distractorRationale.d: Fourth order would give a ratio of 16.

questions.explanation: The observed order is $p=\ln(e_1/e_2)/\ln(h_1/h_2)=\ln4/\ln2=2$. The slope on the log-log plot equals this order, here consistent with the second-order three-point scheme.

questions.stem: A small residual always guarantees a small error in the computed solution of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{b}$, regardless of the condition number of $\mathbf{A}$.
questions.explanation: The relative error can be as large as the condition number times the relative residual, $\|\mathbf{e}\|/\|\mathbf{u}\|\le\kappa\,\|\mathbf{r}\|/\|\mathbf{b}\|$, so for an ill-conditioned matrix a tiny residual may still correspond to a large error in the solution. The residual test must therefore be combined with a check on the solution or the condition number.

questions.stem: A dense $2000\times2000$ matrix of double-precision numbers (8 bytes each) is stored for a 1D diffusion model with 2000 unknowns. How much memory does it need, in MB (1 MB = $10^{6}$ bytes)?
questions.explanation: The matrix has $2000^2=4\times10^{6}$ entries, each 8 bytes, so it needs $3.2\times10^{7}$ bytes = 32.0 MB. A tridiagonal store of $3n$ entries would need only 48 kB.

questions.stem: Apply two Jacobi sweeps to $4x_1-x_2=3$, $-x_1+4x_2-x_3=2$, $-x_2+4x_3=3$ starting from $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$. Give the first component $x_1$ after the second sweep.
questions.explanation: Sweep 1 gives $(0.75,0.50,0.75)$. Sweep 2 uses these old values: $x_1=(3+0.50)/4=0.875$, $x_2=(2+0.75+0.75)/4=0.875$. The exact solution is $(1,1,1)$, so Jacobi is still converging.

questions.stem: A one-dimensional diffusion problem $u''=2$ on $0\le x\le1$ has $u(0)=1$ and $u(1)=3$. Use $h=0.25$ (three interior nodes), assemble the tridiagonal system and solve for $u(0.5)$.
questions.explanation: At each node $u_{i-1}-2u_i+u_{i+1}=2h^2=0.125$. With $u_0=1$ and $u_4=3$ the right-hand side is $(-0.875,\ 0.125,\ -2.875)$, and solving gives $u=(1.3125,\ 1.7500,\ 2.3125)$. This equals the exact solution $x^2+x+1$ at the nodes, since it is a quadratic.

questions.stem: A second-order finite-difference solution has an error of $3.2\times10^{-3}$ at a monitoring point when $h=0.10$ m. Assuming the leading error term dominates, predict the error when $h=0.025$ m, expressed in units of $10^{-4}$.
questions.explanation: The step is reduced by a factor of 4, so the error of a second-order scheme falls by $4^2=16$: $3.2\times10^{-3}/16=0.00020$. A measured ratio far from 16 would suggest the asymptotic regime has not been reached or that boundary conditions are only first-order accurate.

questions.stem: Compare direct and iterative solvers for the sparse symmetric positive-definite systems produced by a fine finite-difference or finite-element mesh. Give at least two advantages of each type and state a typical use.
markingGuide: Direct: fixed operation count, robust, no convergence issues; reuses the factorisation for multiple right-hand sides
Direct: fill-in raises memory and cost for 3D problems; banded/skyline storage reduces it
Iterative: low memory ($O(n)$), no fill-in, cost per iteration proportional to non-zeros
Iterative: convergence rate depends on conditioning, so preconditioning (e.g. incomplete Cholesky, multigrid) is needed; conjugate gradients is the standard choice
Uses: direct for 1D, 2D moderate size; iterative for very large 3D models
questions.explanation: The trade-off is robustness and multiple right-hand sides versus memory and speed on very large systems. Both rely on sparsity, and the right choice depends on mesh dimension, size and conditioning.

questions.stem: For the tridiagonal system from a one-dimensional diffusion problem, describe how you would check the discrete solution against the exact solution and plot the error against step size, and state what slope you expect and why.
markingGuide: Solve on a sequence of grids, e.g. $n=4,8,16,32$ ($h$ halved each time)
Compute the error at a fixed point (or a norm such as the maximum nodal error) against the exact solution
Plot $\log e$ against $\log h$; the slope is the observed order of accuracy
Expect slope 2 for the three-point scheme because truncation error is $O(h^2)$
Departures: first-order boundary treatment, round-off at small $h$, or solver tolerance larger than the truncation error
questions.explanation: The slope on a log-log plot equals the order of accuracy of the scheme. Seeing slope 2 confirms that the implementation, including boundary conditions, matches the theoretical second-order accuracy; a lower slope reveals an error in the discretisation or the tolerance.
